note.text: Read the whole passage before answering. Separate directly stated facts, reasons, proposals and information that remains unknown. An inference needs an identifiable clue and must not turn a fictional case into a universal claim. Notice who speaks and whether a statement is an opinion, a plan or an observed result. This is a written script for listening preparation: no recording is supplied and no hearing or speaking is assessed.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to extract sources and distinguish observation, proposal and measured result. Builds on: environmental discussion and contextual vocabulary. Leads to: concord and careful formal writing.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original script: In a fictional club discussion, a teacher explains that air pollution can come from combustion sources such as motor vehicles, as well as dust. A pupil proposes recording where visible smoke or dust is noticed, with adult guidance and without approaching sources. The teacher says these observations do not measure pollutant concentrations or establish anyone’s diagnosis. The group proposes asking a suitable specialist about available information. No survey result or medical conclusion is supplied.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Locate the relevant sentence, state your answer and identify its support. Check whether a question asks what happened, why, or what cannot be concluded. Then use a teacher-provided oral reading for real listening practice if available.
